prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We shouldn’t raise mixed babiesin the South, Kay says as I drive up the crest of another hill on our way into Kentucky. The South, where humidity leaves a sweat mustache, where a truck with a Confederate flag painted on the back windshield skitters in front of us. In its bed, avoiding our eyes, a boy with blond hair split down the middle like a Bible left open to the Book of Psalms. His shirtless, sun-licked skin drapes, a thin coat for his bones, his clavicles sharp. I want to know who’s driving this raggedy truck. I want the boy to look at us. I want to spray paint a black fist over that flag. I want the truck to find its way into the ravine. I want to— Stepping on the gas, I pass the truck, Kay and I turn our heads. The boy smiles and waves. The man driving doesn’t turn his head, keeps his eyes on the road. Kay turns red as she draws her fingers into fists. I stare at the whites of her eyes.

Keywords: South, Kay, Kentucky

outputs.L1:
“We shouldn’t raise mixed babies in the South,” Kay says as I drive up the crest of another hill on our way into Kentucky. 

The South, where humidity leaves a sweat mustache; where a truck with a Confederate flag painted across the back windshield skitters in front of us. In its bed, avoiding our eyes, sits a boy with blond hair parted down the middle like a Bible left open to the Book of Psalms. His shirtless, sun-licked skin hangs on him, a thin coat for his bones, his clavicles sharp.

I want to know who’s driving this raggedy truck. I want the boy to look at us. I want to spray-paint a Black fist over that flag. I want the truck to find its way into the ravine. I want to—

Stepping on the gas, I pass the truck. Kay and I turn our heads. The boy smiles and waves. The man driving doesn’t turn his head; he keeps his eyes on the road. Kay flushes red as she curls her fingers into fists. I stare at the whites of her eyes.
outputs.L2:
“We can’t bring up mixed-race children in the South,” Kay says while I steer over the top of yet another hill, headed toward Kentucky. This is the South: air so damp it beads sweat above your lip, a pickup ahead of us with a Confederate flag painted across its rear window. In the truck bed sits a blond boy, his hair parted neatly down the center, like a Bible opened to Psalms, and he keeps from meeting our gaze. He has no shirt on; the sun has browned his skin, which hangs lightly over his narrow frame, his collarbones jutting out.

I find myself wondering who is behind the wheel of that beat-up truck. I wish the boy would look our way. I imagine covering the flag with a spray-painted Black power fist. I imagine the truck veering off into the ravine. I want to—

I press harder on the accelerator and pull around the pickup. Kay and I both look over. The boy grins and lifts his hand to wave. The driver, a man, never glances aside; he keeps his attention fixed on the road. Kay’s face flushes red as her hands curl into fists. I look at the white around her eyes.
outputs.L3:
As they drive into Kentucky, Kay says that they should not raise mixed-race children in the South. Her remark hangs over the car, shaped by the landscape around them and by the history the region represents. The narrator becomes acutely aware of the Southern atmosphere: the heavy humidity, the oppressive feeling of the road, and the presence of a pickup truck ahead of them displaying a Confederate flag. The flag is not just a decoration; to the narrator, it becomes a threatening symbol of racism and hostility.

In the back of the truck rides a thin blond boy. At first, he avoids looking at them, and this makes the narrator uneasy. His refusal to meet their eyes seems suspicious, even insulting, and the narrator’s anger begins to build. The sight of the Confederate flag intensifies these feelings, leading the narrator to imagine tearing it down or defacing it. In that moment of rage, the narrator even wishes harm on the truck itself, imagining it damaged or destroyed before they pass it on the road.

Then, unexpectedly, the boy looks up. Instead of glaring or showing hostility, he smiles and waves. The gesture complicates the narrator’s assumptions and interrupts the anger that had been building. Kay, however, reacts with anger, while the driver remains focused on the road, keeping his eyes straight ahead. The moment is brief but charged, revealing the tension between fear, prejudice, historical memory, and the possibility of unexpected human connection.
outputs.L4:
The passage explores the fear and tension surrounding interracial family life in the South through a disturbing encounter on the road. As Kay and her family drive, they notice a truck displaying a Confederate flag, a symbol that immediately triggers anxiety, anger, and painful associations. The scene becomes charged with danger not because anything openly violent happens, but because the flag carries a history of racism, intimidation, and exclusion. Through this brief moment, the passage shows how racism can enter ordinary daily life suddenly and forcefully, turning something as simple as driving down the road into an experience filled with threat.

The author uses vivid sensory imagery to make the encounter feel immediate and uncomfortable. The truck, the flag, the road, and the physical closeness of the vehicles create a sense of pressure and confinement. Kay’s emotional response is equally intense. Her internal monologue reveals anger at the flag and at what it represents, but also fear for her children. Because her children are mixed-race, the symbol is not abstract to her; it feels like a direct warning about the world they must live in. Her thoughts show how deeply racism affects parents who must worry not only about themselves, but also about how their children will be seen, judged, or threatened by others.

One of the most striking moments is the boy’s unexpected smile. Instead of behaving in the openly hostile way Kay anticipates, the boy in the truck smiles at them. This smile creates a sharp contrast with the Confederate flag and complicates the scene. It does not erase the racism associated with the symbol, but it does make the moment less simple. The boy may not fully understand the meaning of the flag, or he may have inherited its symbolism without questioning it. His smile suggests that prejudice is not always expressed through obvious hatred; it can exist alongside innocence, friendliness, ignorance, or contradiction.

This contrast intensifies Kay’s emotional conflict. She is not comforted by the smile, because the flag still represents danger. Instead, the moment deepens her fear and anger. She recognizes that her children are growing up in a place where racist symbols can appear casually and where the people connected to those symbols may not even recognize the harm they cause. The passage therefore reveals the complexity of Southern racism: it is both historical and present, both public and personal, both blatant and hidden beneath ordinary gestures. Through Kay’s reaction, the text captures the emotional burden of raising mixed children in a society where love within the family must constantly confront hatred outside it.
outputs.L5:
In the heart of the South, Kentucky offers a rich blend of history, natural beauty, and warm hospitality. Rolling hills, horse farms, bluegrass music, and small towns give the state its unique charm. From the Appalachian Mountains in the east to the vibrant cities of Louisville and Lexington, Kentucky reflects the spirit and culture of the Southern region.

Kay had always loved Kentucky for its peaceful landscapes and friendly communities. She enjoyed driving along country roads, visiting local festivals, and listening to stories passed down through generations. For her, the South was more than a place on a map—it was a feeling of home, tradition, and connection. Kentucky, with its scenic views and deep cultural roots, remained one of the places that captured that feeling best.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a tense literary fiction excerpt in first person about an interracial couple driving through the rural South, encountering a Confederate flag on a truck, with vivid sensory imagery and internal conflict.
counterfactuals.output:
The road narrowed after the last gas station, where the pumps clicked in the heat and a sun-faded sign promised boiled peanuts, bait, and salvation. I watched the town fall away in the side mirror: cinderblock church, feed store, a dog asleep under a rusted mailbox. Then there was only pine shadow and bright, punishing sky.

Mara drove with both hands on the wheel.

That was the first thing I noticed, or told myself I noticed. Her knuckles had gone pale against the black leather, the silver ring on her thumb flashing each time the road bent and the sun found it. The air conditioner coughed out a weak thread of cold that smelled faintly of mildew. Outside, August pressed its mouth to the windows. Kudzu climbed the trees in green, suffocating sheets, making ghosts of whatever stood still long enough.

I wanted to say something harmless.

Look at that hawk.

Did you see the church sign?

We should stop for peaches.

But language had become a room I could not enter without breaking something.

The truck appeared behind us after a curve, high-bodied and mud-spattered, its grille filling the rearview mirror like a set of teeth. At first it was only another truck. There had been many: white men in caps, trailers loaded with timber, coolers strapped down with orange cord. Then it pulled closer, close enough that I could see the driver’s forearm hanging from the window, sunburned and freckled, close enough that Mara’s eyes flicked up to the mirror and stayed there.

The flag snapped from a pole bolted to the bed.

Red field. Blue cross. White stars.

It cracked in the wind as if delighted with itself.

Something old and bitter rose in me, though I had no right to call it old. My people had arrived later, brown and bewildered, carrying recipes and engineering degrees and the belief that politeness was a kind of armor. Mara’s people had been here long enough to have been buried in fields without names. Between us, in the car, sat all the history I had failed to imagine before I loved her.

The truck surged closer.

Mara eased her foot off the gas.

“Don’t slow down,” I said too quickly.

Her jaw tightened. “I’m not.”

But she was. The speedometer dipped from fifty-eight to fifty-two, then hovered, as if afraid to choose. The road gave no shoulder worth trusting, only a crumble of gravel and then a ditch shining with black water. Pines crowded near. Cicadas screamed from every direction, that metallic, brain-sawing shriek of summer. The flag thrashed in the mirror.

I felt the uselessness of my body acutely: my hands empty in my lap, my voice trapped behind my teeth, my heart behaving as though panic were an action. I wanted to reach for her. I wanted to tell her I would protect her. The thought shamed me with its thinness. From what? With what? A seat belt. A half-charged phone. A graduate degree. Love, that luminous and insufficient thing.

The truck’s horn blared.

Mara flinched, just once, almost imperceptibly, but I saw it. I saw everything: the muscle jumping in her cheek, the sweat at her temple, the way she did not look at me because looking might make the fear visible, and if it became visible then it would become ours.

“Maybe let him pass,” I said.

There it was: the careful suggestion, the reasonable cowardice. My voice sounded like my father’s in airport security lines, in traffic stops, in any room where anger could be costly. Smile. Comply. Survive. Live to be furious later.

Mara gave a laugh with no humor in it. “There’s nowhere to pull over.”

The truck honked again and swung halfway into the opposite lane, then fell back as a blind hill rose ahead. For a moment its shadow slipped over us. The cab filled the mirror. I could see a second face now, broad and indistinct in the passenger seat. Both of them looking down into our little car, into Mara’s dark hands on the wheel, into my brown face turned toward the glass, into whatever story they had already made of us.

My mouth tasted of pennies.

I thought of Mara that morning in the motel bathroom, brushing her teeth in my T-shirt, humming some tune she refused to identify. I thought of her mother’s warning, delivered softly while Mara packed: Baby, just be careful where you stop. I thought of laughing then—not at the warning, never at the warning, but because fear had seemed, from the fluorescent safety of the kitchen, like something we could outdrive.

The road dipped. A stand of cotton opened suddenly on the right, white bolls trembling in the heat, and the sight of it struck me with such force that I looked away. Mara did not.

“Are you okay?” I asked.

“No,” she said.

The word entered the car and took all the air.

I turned toward her, but her eyes stayed forward. In the hard light her profile looked carved, ancient and young at once. She was twenty-nine. She was my wife. She was a woman driving through a place that had learned a thousand ways to tell her she was not safe, and I was beside her, discovering again and again the poverty of being beloved by someone endangered.

The truck swerved left and gunned its engine. For three suspended seconds it ran beside us, huge tires hissing over the yellow line. The passenger leaned out, shouting something the wind tore apart. I caught only pieces—girl, boy, wrong—and then the flag filled my window, snapping so close I could see the frayed threads at its edge, the dirt in the fabric, the cheap plastic clamp trembling on the pole.

Mara kept her eyes on the road.

I did not.

I looked up at the driver, at the mirrored sunglasses, the cap pulled low, the mouth moving around words I would not give the dignity of remembering. He looked back at me and smiled, and in that smile was an invitation: to rage, to fear, to become exactly the small and shaking thing he wanted.

My hand found Mara’s knee.

Not to steady her. I knew that lie immediately.

To steady myself.

For a moment she did not move. Then her fingers left the wheel just long enough to cover mine, warm and damp and real. The truck roared ahead, cut sharply in front of us, and spat gravel from its tires. A stone cracked against the windshield with a sound like a gunshot.

I ducked.

Mara did not. Her hand returned to the wheel. The windshield held, marked now by a white starburst low on my side, no larger than a quarter. Through it the road wavered and split.

The truck sped away, flag shrinking, still frantic in the hot wind.

Neither of us spoke until it was gone around the next bend. Even then, silence remained, dense as smoke. The cicadas screamed. The air conditioner rattled. Somewhere beyond the trees, unseen water rotted sweetly in a ditch.

“I’m sorry,” I said at last.

Mara looked at me then, quick and sharp, not unkind. “For what?”

I had no answer that was not too large or too small.

For being afraid.

For thinking fear could be shared evenly.

For believing, before this road, that loving you meant I understood the country better than I did.

So I watched the pines streak past, their shadows striping her face, and said nothing. The cracked place in the glass caught the sun and burned white between us.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a short scene in the style of contemporary Southern Gothic prose where two women named Kay and the narrator enter Kentucky and confront racism symbolized by a truck with a Confederate flag.
counterfactuals.output:
By the time Kay and I crossed into Kentucky, the sky had gone the color of old bruises, purple at the edges and yellow where the sun was trying to die. The road unspooled between fields gone flat and winter-brown, past barns leaning like they’d heard bad news and never recovered.

Kay drove with both hands on the wheel. She always did when she was angry.

We saw the truck at the gas station just over the state line, backed into a space like it owned the place. Mud caked the tires. A rifle rack showed in the rear window. From the bed rose a Confederate flag, snapping hard in the wind, red as a fresh slap.

Nobody had to say what it meant.

Kay cut the engine but didn’t get out. The pumps ticked and hummed. Somewhere behind the station, a dog barked once, then seemed to think better of it.

A white man in a seed cap stood by the truck, watching us through the smoke of his cigarette. His eyes moved over Kay, then over me, slow and measuring, as if we were trespassing not on asphalt but on history itself.

Kay opened her door.

“Don’t,” I said, though I didn’t know if I meant don’t get gas, don’t look at him, or don’t let this place turn you into a ghost before my eyes.

She stepped out anyway. The wind caught her coat and lifted it like wings. For one second she looked less like a woman and more like judgment arriving in sensible shoes.

The man flicked ash onto the concrete.

Kay stared at the flag until it cracked above us, bright and ugly against the bruised sky.

“My grandmother used to say,” she said quietly, “some folks hang their shame up high so God won’t miss it.”

The man’s mouth tightened. He didn’t answer.

Inside the station, the fluorescent lights buzzed like trapped insects. The cashier pretended to count cigarettes. I pumped the gas with hands gone cold, every click of the nozzle sounding too loud, like bones being set.

When we pulled away, the flag was still there in the mirror, whipping itself into a fury.

Kay didn’t look back.

But I did. And for miles afterward, I could feel it following us—not cloth, not color, but the old thing underneath, risen from the dirt and riding the road behind our car, hungry as ever.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a lyrical, emotionally charged paragraph about a road trip into the American South, including humidity, a child in the back of a pickup, and the narrator’s violent intrusive thoughts before an unexpected wave.
counterfactuals.output: The farther we drove into the American South, the more the humidity rose around us like a living thing, pressing its wet hands to the windows, blurring the pines and kudzu into one green, breathing wall. Ahead, the road shimmered under the sun, and in the back of a rust-red pickup, a child stood barefoot among coolers and feed sacks, hair whipping wild, one small hand lifted as if blessing every passing car. I watched them through the windshield and felt, with shame and terror, the sudden flare of my own violent intrusive thoughts—bright, unwanted, senseless as lightning behind the eyes—then gripped my knees until they passed, leaving me hollow and sweating. We crossed through towns with names like hymns, past gas stations, church signs, fields sagging under the heat, until the land broke open without warning and an unexpected wave of salt air rolled over the highway, carrying gull cries and the dark blue promise of water.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a flash fiction passage beginning with “We shouldn’t raise mixed babies in the South, Kay says” and continue it with poetic description, racial tension, and a complicated moment of human recognition.
counterfactuals.output:
“We shouldn’t raise mixed babies in the South, Kay says,” and the cicadas take it up like a dare, grinding their glass wings in the oak trees until the whole yard seems to buzz with warning.

She is standing on the porch in her bare feet, one hand pressed to the swell beneath her dress, the other worrying the hem like a rosary. Across the road, Mr. Pritchard’s flag hangs limp in the heat. The ditch is full of Queen Anne’s lace and beer cans, white blossoms floating over rusted mouths.

“You mean we shouldn’t,” I say.

Kay looks past me to the cotton field gone silver under the moon. “I mean the world shouldn’t be like this.”

Down at the gas station that morning, a woman had stared too long at Kay’s belly, then at me, then at the wedding band on my hand as if it were counterfeit. Her little boy, red-faced and sticky with cola, had asked, “What color’s the baby gonna be?” and his mother had slapped his arm so hard the sound cracked open the aisle. Not because he was cruel. Because he had said the quiet thing out loud.

Kay had left without the milk.

Now the night presses close, smelling of honeysuckle and wet dirt, of something sweet rotting in the fence line. I want to tell her we can go north, west, anywhere the maps promise a different kind of weather. But every place I name has its own locked doors, its own whispering counters, its own old men teaching children how to look.

A truck slows on the road. For a second we both go still. Headlights drag over us—her pale face, my dark hands, the round insistence between us. The driver is Mr. Pritchard himself, ancient and narrow as a fence post. He looks, and I feel my body preparing: jaw tight, shoulders squared, the old arithmetic of danger adding itself in my blood.

Then his truck coughs and dies.

Silence.

He sits there with both hands on the wheel. Kay exhales first. I walk down because not walking down would be fear, and walking down might be foolishness, and in this place those are often twins.

“You need a hand?” I ask.

Mr. Pritchard does not answer right away. His eyes flick to the porch, to Kay. Something moves over his face—not kindness, not quite shame. Recognition, maybe, arriving late and poorly dressed.

“My Alice,” he says at last, so softly I almost miss it. “She used to stand just like that when she was carrying.”

I lift the hood. Steam breathes out, ghost-white. Behind me, Kay comes down the steps and stands in the road, one hand under her belly, the other shading her eyes from the headlights.

For a few minutes, the three of us bend toward the ruined engine as if it were a common grief, as if heat and metal and the stubborn need to get home could make a country.

When the truck starts again, Mr. Pritchard nods once. He does not bless us. He does not apologize. He drives away slow, taillights red as two wounds disappearing into the dark.

Kay takes my hand.

Inside her, the baby turns—small, alive, already listening.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a first-person prose scene about Kay and the narrator passing a raggedy truck with a Confederate flag, exploring fear, anger, and tenderness through detailed imagery and fragmented thoughts.
counterfactuals.output:
Kay saw the truck before I did.

Her hand tightened on my knee—just once, a quick animal pressure—and then she let go like she hadn’t meant to touch me. Like the touch had escaped.

Ahead of us, in the right lane, the truck rattled along with one brake light dead and the bed sagging under a heap of scrap wood, rusted chain, a blue tarp snapping loose at one corner. The tailgate was the color of dried blood where the paint had flaked off. A sticker peeled from the bumper in dirty curls. And from a pole bolted behind the cab, a Confederate flag whipped in the hot air, bright as a fresh bruise.

For a second the road narrowed.

Not really. It was still four lanes, shimmering with noon heat, gas stations and pawnshops slipping by, the sky too wide and white over everything. But inside the car—inside my chest—there was suddenly less room.

Kay sat very still.

She had been laughing a minute before. Something about the woman in the rest stop restroom who’d been brushing her teeth with such violence, foam on her chin, eyes on herself in the mirror like she was preparing for war. Kay had done the impression, shoulders hunched, wrist sawing back and forth, and I had laughed so hard I missed the first green light.

Now her mouth was closed. Her sunglasses hid her eyes, but I knew the shape of her looking. Forward. Not at the truck exactly. Past it. Through it.

The flag snapped and folded and snapped again.

Cloth. Just cloth, I told myself.

But not just cloth.

Never just.

My fingers found the wheel at ten and two like I was sixteen again, like somebody stern was grading me. The truck’s exhaust coughed black into the lane. It smelled like oil and old pennies, like a garage floor after rain. I thought about passing. I thought about staying behind. I thought about the two men visible through the rear window, caps low, shoulders broad. One of them lifted a hand to scratch the back of his neck.

A harmless movement.

A hand becoming anything.

My pulse thudded in my throat.

“Don’t,” Kay said.

“I didn’t say anything.”

“I know.”

Her voice was soft, but not gentle. Flat with knowledge. The kind you get tired of having.

The flag cracked hard in the wind.

I felt anger rise in me, quick and stupid, a match struck too close to dry grass. Anger at the truck, at the men in it, at the flag, at every person who had ever pretended not to know what it meant. Anger at the road for containing us together. Anger at myself for being afraid and then angry at Kay for being calm, except she wasn’t calm, and I knew that, and the shame of knowing it made my face burn.

I wanted to say something brave.

Something clean and bright.

Fuck them.

I’m not scared.

Let’s pass them.

Let’s make them see us.

But bravery in my mouth tasted like metal. Like a dare someone else would have to survive.

Kay turned her head slightly toward the window. Sunlight moved over her cheekbone, over the small scar near her ear from when she fell off her cousin’s bike at nine. She had told me that story the first night she slept over, her hair spread across my pillow, her finger tracing the scar like punctuation. I’d wanted to kiss it then but didn’t. Later, when I knew I was allowed, I did. Softly. She laughed and said, “You’re so dramatic,” but she didn’t move away.

Now the scar was a pale comma in the heat.

A pause.

The truck drifted toward the center line, then corrected. The flag leaned with the motion, its red field buckling. I could see where the fabric had frayed at the edges, strings coming loose, unraveling in plain sight and still held high.

My foot eased off the gas.

Kay noticed.

“We can pass,” she said.

“You said don’t.”

“I meant don’t start.”

“I wasn’t going to start.”

She breathed out through her nose. Almost a laugh. Almost not.

The tenderness came then, inconvenient and aching. It slid under the anger, under the fear, and made them both heavier. I wanted to cover her with my body, which was ridiculous—we were in a car, moving seventy miles an hour, and my body was not a shield against history, or guns, or the sudden meanness of strangers. I wanted to reach for her hand, but I didn’t know if touch would comfort her or make the fear more real. I wanted to say her name in a way that could build a room around it.

Kay.

Instead I checked the mirror.

A minivan behind us. A motorcycle farther back. The left lane open.

The truck spat gravel from one tire. Tiny stones pinged against our windshield like thrown seeds.

Kay flinched.

There. So small I might have missed it if I didn’t love her. The quick tightening around her mouth. The lift of one shoulder. Then gone.

My anger changed shape.

No flame now. Something colder. A stone in water.

I put on the blinker.

The click filled the car, absurdly polite.

Tick.

Tick.

Tick.

We moved into the left lane.

As we drew alongside the truck, time stretched thin. I saw the passenger’s elbow hanging out the window, sunburned and freckled, a cigarette pinched between two fingers. I saw the driver’s jaw working on gum. I saw an empty fast-food cup rolling on the dashboard, a cracked phone mount, a strip of duct tape holding the side mirror together. Human details. Ordinary. That made it worse somehow. Monsters should announce themselves. They should glow sulfur-yellow, drag claws, carry signs.

But men could be men.

A flag could be a flag.

A threat could ride beside you in daylight, obeying the speed limit.

Kay turned her face away before they could look in. Or maybe before she could look back. Her hand rested on the center console, fingers curled inward, nails short and painted chipped blue. Without thinking, I laid my hand over hers.

She did not pull away.

Her skin was warm. Damp at the palm. Alive.

The passenger glanced over.

I felt it like a touch at the base of my neck.

Don’t speed. Don’t slow. Don’t give him anything. Don’t make yourself small. Don’t get us killed. Don’t be dramatic. Don’t be foolish. Don’t let him know. Let him know. Let him know nothing. Let him know we are here.

The thoughts came broken, colliding.

White stripe. Red field. Blue cross. Smoke. Sun. Kay’s hand.

The passenger looked at us for one second, maybe two. His face did nothing. Or I couldn’t read it. Then his head turned forward again and the truck fell back, inch by inch, its engine groaning like something dragged from a ditch.

We passed.

That was all.

No shouted word. No thrown bottle. No chase. No cinematic justice. Just the truck receding in the mirror, flag still snapping, still there, still loud even as it shrank.

My shoulders hurt from holding them tight.

Kay squeezed my hand.

I looked over.

She had pushed her sunglasses up into her hair. Her eyes were wet, but she wasn’t crying. Or she was doing the version of crying that keeps moving through the world because stopping is a luxury, because there is always another mile, another exit, another man with a symbol, another room where someone says it’s heritage, another day where the body remembers before the mind gives permission.

“You okay?” I asked.

A stupid question. A necessary one.

She nodded, then shook her head, then nodded again.

“I hate that thing,” she said.

“I know.”

“No.” Her voice cracked—not loud, just split down the center. “I hate how it makes me feel. Like I’m already running.”

I brought her hand to my mouth and kissed the backs of her fingers. Once. Briefly. The road hummed beneath us.

“You’re here,” I said.

It wasn’t enough. It was almost nothing.

But Kay closed her eyes.

“I’m here,” she repeated.

The fields opened on either side of the highway, yellow-green and blurred at the edges. A line of blackbirds lifted from a wire all at once, scattering into the white sky like ash shaken from a page. The truck was far behind us now, swallowed by heat waves and traffic, but the fear did not disappear. It loosened. It moved to the back seat. It sat there breathing.

So did the anger.

So did tenderness, stubborn and quiet, her hand still inside mine.

We drove on.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
